title: How to become a foster carer in the UK: from first enquiry to first placement
standfirst: Who you can apply to, what the checks and assessment involve, how long approval usually takes, and what support and pay look like once a child is placed with you.

sections.heading: The journey in brief
paragraphs: Forms, timescales and some rules differ between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, so treat this guide as a map rather than a timetable.
bullets: Enquiry and an initial home visit
Preparation training
Checks and a social work assessment
Fostering panel and the service's decision
Matching, your first placement and ongoing support

sections.heading: Who can apply
paragraphs: For England, gov.uk says you must be at least 18 (most services ask for 21 or over), have the right to work in the UK and be able to care for a child, often full time. You do not need to own your home, but you will usually need a spare bedroom. Scotland's mygov.scot guidance adds that there is no upper age limit and that renting, having your own children or working full time do not rule you out, though some councils restrict certain types of fostering to full-time workers. Marital status, sexual orientation and religion cannot count against you. Services look for people who can nurture a child and work as part of a team.

sections.heading: Step 1: decide who to apply to
paragraphs: You apply through a fostering service: your local council's fostering team (in Northern Ireland, your Health and Social Care Trust) or an independent fostering agency (IFA), which may be a charity or a company. You can only be registered with one service at a time, so speak to two or three first.

Councils are responsible for children in care and place them with their own carers first, turning to agencies only when no in-house carer is free. Foster Wales says this makes council carers more likely to be considered for all ages, including babies, and to care for local children, while agency carers tend to have slightly older children, sometimes from further away, with gaps between placements. A long-standing piece on The Fostering Network's site notes that agencies often offer more supervising social worker time and higher allowances.

Any service must be registered with the regulator: Ofsted in England, the Care Inspectorate in Scotland, Care Inspectorate Wales or the RQIA in Northern Ireland. Read its latest inspection report, and ask:
bullets: Will the social worker who assesses you also supervise you afterwards?
What does the year's training programme look like?
What are the allowance and any fee, and what happens between placements?

sections.heading: Step 2: enquiry, home visit and preparation training
paragraphs: The service will talk through the types of fostering, then usually visit your home to see the room a child would use and meet everyone who lives with you. You will be invited to a preparation course, before or alongside your assessment. In Wales this is typically a free two-day Skills to Foster course; in Scotland, preparation groups led by experienced carers are compulsory. You can withdraw at any stage, and applying is normally free.

sections.heading: Step 3: the assessment
paragraphs: In England the assessment has two stages. Stage one is the practical checks: enhanced DBS checks with barred lists for you and every adult in your household, a medical report usually from your GP, local authority and employer checks, contact with previous significant partners, at least two references, and a health and safety check of your home. If the service decides not to continue after stage one, it must write to you with reasons within 10 days of receiving all the stage one information.

Stage two is about you: your personality and relationship history, ethnicity, culture and beliefs, your willingness to care for a child from a different background, your employment history and standard of living, and any experience of caring for children. An assessing social worker visits regularly, involving your own children if you have them, and writes a report. Many services in England use CoramBAAF's Form F, revised in May 2025 to be more strengths-based and trauma-informed. It recommends whether you should be approved and on what terms: type of fostering, number of children and age range. You read it, add comments and sign it. Scotland and Northern Ireland run similar checks without the two-stage label.

sections.heading: Step 4: panel and the decision
paragraphs: Your report goes to a fostering panel at least five working days before it meets. Panels typically include experienced foster carers, social workers and other independent professionals. You attend with your assessing social worker and answer questions. The panel recommends; the service's agency decision maker, usually a senior manager, decides. Fosterline says that should happen within seven days of receiving the panel minutes, with the outcome given verbally within two days and in writing within five working days. In Scotland, mygov.scot describes the panel itself as making the approval decision.

sections.heading: If you are turned down
paragraphs: Outright rejection at panel is rare: Ofsted recorded 30 in England in 2024 to 2025, against 1,115 applications withdrawn by services, so an early 'not now' is more common. In England, if the service proposes not to approve you, you have 28 days from the date of the letter to make representations or apply to the Independent Review Mechanism, whose panel makes a fresh recommendation that the decision maker must consider. Wales has IRM Cymru, run by Children in Wales, which takes applications for up to 40 days. In Scotland and Northern Ireland, ask your council or Trust fostering team for the reasons and how to appeal.

sections.heading: How long does it take?
paragraphs: For England, gov.uk says up to eight months from application to decision, and the national minimum standards require an assessment to reach panel within eight months of starting. Fosterline estimates four to six months from formal application; Foster Wales Swansea quotes four to six months from first enquiry; mygov.scot gives six to 12 months for Scotland. The usual delays are your own availability, slow references and GP medicals, so chase these early.

sections.heading: After approval: your first placement
paragraphs: Once approved you start post-approval training and meet your supervising social worker. You are sent profiles of children who might suit you and can set preferences on age, gender and type of fostering, but you cannot pick a child out of a group and there is no trial period. Where possible you meet the child first; emergency placements can come with less than 24 hours' notice. When a child arrives you should be told about their background, health and education needs and given a placement plan setting out which day-to-day decisions you can make (delegated authority). You can end a placement with 28 days' notice.

sections.heading: Support and money once you are fostering
paragraphs: You will have two social workers: the child's, and your own supervising social worker. Your service should also offer an out-of-hours advice line, support groups, a personal development plan reviewed yearly, and the chance to take a break. In England a social worker should visit in the child's first week, then every six weeks during the first year; new carers complete the Training, Support and Development Standards workbook within 12 months of approval; and your approval is reviewed at least once a year, with the first review going back to panel.

Money comes in two parts: an allowance for each child's food, clothes, travel and household costs, and a fee that some services pay for your skills and time. For England, gov.uk's minimum weekly allowance for 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027 runs from £176 (a child aged 0 to 2, outside London and the South East) to £309 (16 to 17, London). You register as self-employed with HMRC and claim qualifying care relief, a tax-free amount per household plus relief for each week a child is with you. Fosterline and Fosterline Scotland give free, independent advice on all of this.

nations.England: The Fostering Services (England) Regulations 2011 and national minimum standards apply. Independent agencies must register with Ofsted. The 2026 to 2027 minimum allowance is £176 to £309 a week depending on the child's age and your area, and a proposed refusal can go to the Independent Review Mechanism within 28 days. Fosterline: 0800 040 7675.
nations.Scotland: Apply through one of the 32 councils, an independent agency or a charity, all registered with the Care Inspectorate. Preparation groups are compulsory. After approval you sign a foster carer agreement and are reviewed by panel after your first year, then every two years. Councils must pay at least the Scottish Recommended Allowance: from 1 April 2026, £177.68 a week for a child aged 0 to 4, £206.71 for 5 to 15 and £283.35 for 16 and over. Fosterline Scotland: 0141 204 1400.
nations.Wales: Foster Wales is the Welsh Government-backed network of all 22 council fostering services; Care Inspectorate Wales regulates. Every council has signed the National Commitment package of training, support and rewards. The Fostering Network lists the Welsh national minimum allowance for 2026 to 2027 as £229 (0 to 4), £208 (5 to 15) and £260 (16 to 17) a week. Refusals can be reviewed by IRM Cymru within 40 days. Foster Wales states that from 2027 for-profit agencies will not be able to recruit new foster carers in Wales.
nations.Northern Ireland: Children in care are the responsibility of the five Health and Social Care Trusts, each with a fostering service supported by HSC NI Adoption and Foster Care; independent providers also operate. The RQIA is the regulator. There is no maximum age, checks include AccessNI, and applications go to a fostering panel. nidirect's published rates from 1 April 2024 run from £149 a week (0 to 4) to £219 (16 and over); The Fostering Network reports uplifts since, so ask your Trust. Trust carers get 24-hour fostering social work support, short breaks and annual reviews.

faq.question: Can I foster if I rent, am single, work full time or have my own children?
faq.answer: In principle, yes. Official guidance across the UK says you need not own your home, and Scotland's and Northern Ireland's add that you can be single or in a couple and in work or not. The practical tests are a spare bedroom and availability; some services limit full-time workers to certain types of fostering.

faq.question: Can I apply to more than one fostering service at once?
faq.answer: No. gov.uk and Foster Wales both say you can only be registered with one service at a time. Talk to several before choosing; approved carers can transfer later.

faq.question: What is the difference between an allowance and a fee?
faq.answer: The allowance is paid weekly for each child to cover their costs, and every carer with a child in placement gets one. A fee is an extra payment some services make for your skills and time; it is not required by law and varies, so ask for a written breakdown.

faq.question: Do I get to choose which children I foster?
faq.answer: You set preferences such as age range and type of fostering during assessment, and these become your terms of approval. The service then sends you profiles of children who may suit you, and you can say if a match is not right, but you cannot pick a child from a group and there is no trial period.

title: Who can foster: eligibility and requirements in the UK
standfirst: What you actually need to become a foster carer in the UK: age, housing, relationships, work, health, criminal record checks, pets, smoking and immigration status, plus the myths that put people off applying.

sections.heading: The short answer
paragraphs: Far fewer people are ruled out of fostering than most assume. The law sets only a handful of hard limits; almost everything else is decided through an assessment of you, your home and the people you live with. Each fostering service, council or independent, adds its own policies on top, so the honest answer to many questions is: it depends on the service and the type of fostering.

sections.heading: Age: a minimum, but no maximum
paragraphs: Government guidance for England says you must be at least 18, though most services want you to be at least 21. Scotland's mygov.scot guidance is the same: 18 or over, with some agencies not accepting anyone under 21. The Fostering Network notes there is no legal lower age limit as such, so a service turning away someone aged 18 or over purely on age should be able to justify it. Services can set their own bar; Surrey County Council, for example, asks for over 21.

There is no upper age limit anywhere in the UK: The Fostering Network says there is no legal maximum, and guidance for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland says the same. What is assessed is whether you are fit and well enough to meet the needs of the children you would care for, not your date of birth.

sections.heading: Housing and the spare room question
paragraphs: You do not need to own your home. Renting is fine if your tenancy is secure; services typically want a stable tenancy agreement and may ask for your landlord's written permission. A large house is not required. The assessment looks for a safe, stable home with space for a child.

The spare bedroom is the requirement people most often stumble on, and for most fostering it is a real one. In England the national minimum standards say each fostered child over the age of three should have their own bedroom. Sharing is allowed only where a separate room is genuinely not possible, the child's responsible authority agrees and each child has their own area within the room, after the service has weighed any risk of bullying, any history of abuse and the children's wishes. A baby under two can sleep in the carers' bedroom. Short-break carers may only need a room for the nights a child stays, and in Scotland some councils make exceptions depending on the child's age. If your spare room is small or doubles as an office, raise it early rather than assuming you are ruled out.

sections.heading: Relationship status and family
paragraphs: You can foster whether you are single, married, in a civil partnership, cohabiting, divorced or widowed. Single applicants are assessed on the same basis as couples, with attention to the support network around them. Sexual orientation and gender identity are not relevant; Scottish guidance says fostering is open to you regardless of any protected characteristic under the Equality Act, such as marital status, sexual orientation or religion. A new partner is not a problem in itself, but any partner involved in caring for a child must be assessed and approved alongside you. You do not need children of your own, though services want to see some relevant experience of children.

sections.heading: Work, income and benefits
paragraphs: Whether you can keep working depends on the child's circumstances and the service. Part-time work is often workable, particularly with school-age children, but full-time day care for a fostered child is not usually considered appropriate, and for babies, pre-school children and parent-and-child placements some services require one carer at home full time. Supported lodgings and short breaks sit more comfortably alongside a full-time job.

Being unemployed or on benefits does not stop you fostering. Services look at your finances for stability rather than a salary threshold. Three practical points: there is no statutory right to time off work for fostering; councils such as Surrey ask carers to register as self-employed with HMRC; and a fostering allowance can affect some benefit claims, so check with the service and the relevant benefits office first.

sections.heading: Health and disability
paragraphs: Every applicant has a medical, normally a confidential GP report to the service's medical adviser. Its purpose is to check you are physically and emotionally well enough to look after a child day to day, not to find perfect health. A long-term condition, regular medication, a disability or a history of mental health difficulties does not disqualify you; the report is one part of the assessment, and some councils actively encourage disabled applicants.

sections.heading: Criminal record checks: DBS, Disclosure Scotland and AccessNI
paragraphs: Every service must run criminal record checks on you and the other adults in your household. In England this is an enhanced DBS check including the children's barred list, which the regulations require for the applicant and every household member aged 18 or over; Wales uses the same DBS system. In Scotland foster carers join Disclosure Scotland's PVG scheme, and councils also run enhanced checks on household members aged 16 or over. In Northern Ireland it is an enhanced AccessNI check alongside a social services check.

An enhanced check shows spent as well as unspent convictions, cautions and other non-court disposals, relevant police information, and whether you are barred from working with children. Some old and minor matters are filtered out, and fixed penalty tickets and parking fines are not included.

sections.heading: What does and does not rule you out
paragraphs: In England the law is specific. A service must not approve you if you, or an adult in your household, has a conviction or caution for a specified offence committed at 18 or over: an offence against a child, an offence listed in Schedule 4 of the Fostering Services (England) Regulations 2011 (rape and other serious sexual offences, including indecent images of children), or any other offence involving bodily injury to a child other than common assault or battery. The only exception is where a particular child's welfare requires it and you are a relative of that child or already their foster carer.

Everything else is judged on its merits. The Fostering Network says minor offences should not count against you; Scottish government guidance says convictions will not necessarily prevent approval but need careful consideration; and councils such as Surrey and South Lanarkshire say the same, though Surrey's own policy also bars serious violent crime. What matters is what happened, how long ago, what has changed and whether you were honest. Enhanced checks show spent convictions, so declare everything at the start: an undisclosed matter that later surfaces is a far bigger problem than the offence itself.

sections.heading: Pets
paragraphs: Having a pet does not stop you fostering. Each animal is assessed for temperament and behaviour as part of the home assessment, and a pet that is aggressive or has harmed someone may affect approval. Otherwise services generally see pets as a positive part of family life.

sections.heading: Smoking and vaping
paragraphs: There is no UK-wide rule; each service sets its own policy, and Foster Wales notes that these cover e-cigarettes and vaping too. The consistent expectation is a smoke-free home. In practice many services will not place children under five, or children with certain health conditions, with a household where anyone smokes; Surrey, for example, allows older children only where smoking or vaping happens strictly outside and away from children. Smokers are usually offered help to stop.

sections.heading: Immigration status and residency
paragraphs: You do not need to be a British citizen. The requirements set out for England and by The Fostering Network are that you live in the UK and have the right to work here, and services generally expect a full-time UK resident; some councils spell this out as indefinite leave to remain, settled status or permanent residency. If your leave is time-limited a service may still consider you, but will weigh the time and cost of approving someone who may not be able to stay. You need not be a native English speaker, but you will need a good level of spoken and written English. A fostering service cannot advise on your immigration position; for that you need a regulated immigration adviser or solicitor.

sections.heading: Myths that stop people applying
paragraphs: Most people who never apply are stopped by something they assume rather than something they have checked.
bullets: "I'm too old." There is no upper age limit anywhere in the UK.
"I'd need to own a big house." You can rent, and size matters far less than a safe spare room.
"I have to be in a couple." Single people foster and are assessed on the same basis.
"I need to have raised my own children." Not required; relevant experience of children helps.
"I'm gay, or trans, so I won't be considered." Sexual orientation and gender identity are not factors.
"I don't drive." Not required if you have good public transport or support for school runs and appointments.
"My religion will count against me." It will not; carers of all faiths and none foster.
"Any criminal record rules me out." Only a narrow set of offences does.
"I'm on benefits." Receiving benefits does not stop you fostering.
"I have a health condition." What is assessed is whether you are well enough for the role.

sections.heading: Next steps
paragraphs: If nothing here has ruled you out, speak to more than one fostering service, ask each directly about its policies on the points above, and be candid about anything you are unsure of. Honesty at the enquiry stage saves months later.

nations.England: Government guidance: at least 18 (most services require 21), the right to work in the UK and usually a spare bedroom. The Fostering Services (England) Regulations 2011 set the mandatory bar for specified offences and require an enhanced DBS check for the applicant and every household member aged 18 or over, plus a medical report and two personal referees. National minimum standards expect each fostered child over three to have their own bedroom unless sharing is formally agreed.
nations.Scotland: mygov.scot: 18 or over (some agencies insist on 21), no upper age limit, full-time UK resident, and a spare bedroom, with some councils making exceptions by the child's age. The assessment covers medical history, criminal record, finances and home, can take 6 to 12 months and ends with a fostering panel; reviews follow after the first year and then every two years. Checks run through Disclosure Scotland's PVG scheme, and councils also check household members aged 16 or over.
nations.Wales: Foster Wales: no upper age limit, rent or own, a spare room needed, pets assessed rather than barred, and single, LGBTQ+, working and unemployed applicants all welcome. It sets no national minimum age, and smoking and vaping policies vary by local authority, so ask your local Foster Wales team. Criminal record checks use the DBS, as in England.
nations.Northern Ireland: nidirect: no maximum age; single, married or living with a partner; with or without your own children; in or out of work; owning or renting; whatever your race, religion or sexuality. Applicants have a GP medical, an enhanced AccessNI check and a social services check, give references and are assessed by a social worker before a fostering panel makes a recommendation. Fostering is provided by the five HSC trusts and independent providers such as Barnardo's and Action for Children.

faq.question: Can I foster if I'm single?
faq.answer: Yes. Single people foster across the UK and are assessed on the same basis as couples. The service will want to see a support network around you, and any new partner who later helps care for a child will need to be assessed too.

faq.question: Do I really need a spare bedroom?
faq.answer: For most types of fostering, yes. In England each fostered child over three should normally have their own bedroom, with sharing formally agreed by the child's responsible authority. A baby under two can sleep in your room, short-break carers may only need a room for overnight stays, and some Scottish councils make exceptions by age.

faq.question: I have an old conviction. Will it stop me?
faq.answer: Only a narrow group of offences automatically bars you: in England, offences against children, specified sexual offences and offences involving injury to a child, whether by you or an adult in your household. Anything else is considered in context. Enhanced checks show spent convictions, so disclose everything at the start.

faq.question: Can I foster if I rent?
faq.answer: Yes. Guidance in all four UK nations says you do not need to own your home. Services look for a secure tenancy, may ask for your landlord's written permission, and apply the same safety and space checks as to any other home.

faq.question: Can I work full time and foster?
faq.answer: Sometimes, depending on the child and the service. Part-time work alongside school-age children is often possible, but full-time day care for a fostered child is not usually accepted, and for babies and parent-and-child placements some services require a carer at home full time. Short breaks and supported lodgings are the most work-compatible options.

faq.question: Can I foster if I smoke or vape?
faq.answer: Possibly, with limits. Policies vary by service and often cover vaping as well as smoking. Children are expected to live in a smoke-free home, and many services will not place under-fives or children with certain health conditions with a smoking household. Help to stop is usually offered.

title: The fostering assessment and approval process explained
standfirst: From the first home visit to the fostering panel, the agency decision and your first annual review: what happens, how long it takes, and what you can do if you are not approved.

sections.heading: It starts with an enquiry and an initial visit
paragraphs: Every fostering journey begins with an enquiry to a fostering service: your local council (in Northern Ireland, your Health and Social Care Trust) or an independent agency. In England you can only be registered with one service at a time, so talk to more than one first. Most services send an information pack, then arrange a call with a social worker and a home visit, though some use calls or group meetings.

The visit is informal but matters. The social worker will talk through your household, motivation, work and spare room, and answer your questions, so both sides can decide whether fostering is realistic. If you want to go ahead, you complete a formal application and the assessment begins.

sections.heading: Stage 1: checks and references
paragraphs: In England the law splits the assessment into two stages under regulation 26 of the Fostering Services (England) Regulations 2011 and its statutory guidance, and the stages can run one after the other or side by side. Stage 1 gathers the facts and checks a service needs to be sure there is no reason you cannot foster:

The service also checks its own records and the council's where you live, and usually asks your employer for a reference. A service that approved you in the last 12 months must provide a written reference, and Form F covers former partners too.

Stage 1 has a deadline. Once the service holds all the information, it must decide within 10 working days whether you can continue, and if not must give written reasons. There is no independent review of a Stage 1 decision, though you can complain about how your application was handled.
bullets: Your name, address and date of birth, and any current or previous marriage, civil partnership or similar relationship
Everyone else in your household, and your own children whether or not they live with you
Your home
A health report, usually from your GP
Any earlier application to foster, adopt or childmind
An enhanced DBS check for you and every household member aged 18 or over
Two personal referees, whom the service must interview

sections.heading: Preparation training
paragraphs: A preparation course is a standard step across the UK. The most widely used is The Fostering Network's The Skills to Foster, revised in 2025, with six sessions: what children need, fostering relationships, a protective and loving home, therapeutic care, supporting identity, and transitions and endings. The open-access version takes three days, as does Foster Wales's course. Some services add first aid and safeguarding training.
Some councils run it before you apply, others during the assessment; gov.uk lists it as a required step.

sections.heading: Stage 2: the Form F assessment
paragraphs: Stage 2 is the part most people picture: a series of visits from an assessing social worker over several months, written up in England on CoramBAAF's Form F, updated in 2025 to focus more on strengths and the child's needs. The regulations require this stage to cover your personality; your religion and ability to care for a child of a particular faith; your ethnic, cultural and linguistic background; your employment, standard of living and interests; your experience of caring for children; and your skills and potential as a carer.

Expect questions about your family history, past and present relationships, education and work, your typical week, commitments and finances. Councils say the questions are detailed and personal, and that honesty is essential. Other adults in the household need their own checks and references, and councils advise talking to your own children early because fostering affects everyone at home. CoramBAAF says Form F is worked through with you, not a questionnaire to complete alone.

When the report is finished you must be given a copy and 10 working days to add written observations, which go to panel with it. If serious concerns emerge part-way through, the service can instead prepare a brief report and ask the panel whether to stop; you get the same 10 working days to respond.

sections.heading: The fostering panel
paragraphs: The fostering panel is a group of people with an independent chair who read the report and make a recommendation. In England, Scotland and Wales every fostering service must have one; in Northern Ireland panels are usual practice rather than a legal requirement. Members typically include social workers, foster carers, people with care experience and health or education professionals.

You will be invited, usually with your assessing social worker, and should get notice and support to prepare. Members will have read everything and will ask about your assessment, training and the fostering you hope to do; you can ask questions too. The panel then recommends whether you should be approved and on what terms, such as the number and ages of children. It recommends; it does not decide.

sections.heading: The agency decision maker
paragraphs: The decision rests with the agency decision maker (ADM), a senior member of staff who must decide personally and cannot delegate, taking the panel's recommendation into account. In England the statutory guidance expects a decision within seven working days of receiving the panel minutes, with reasons recorded. In Scotland the decision must be made within 14 days of the panel and notified within seven days.
If approved, you sign a foster carer agreement setting out what the service will provide and what it expects of you, and join its list of carers available for matching.

sections.heading: How long does it take?
paragraphs: It depends largely on how quickly checks come back. Gov.uk says the English process can take up to eight months, and the statutory guidance expects the panel's recommendation within eight months of your application. CoramBAAF and Foster Wales both describe a typical assessment as around six months, and Scottish guidance says authorities should normally aim to finish within six months of an application. Some councils publish targets of four to six months or about 20 weeks. A DBS check alone can take around eight weeks, longer if you have lived abroad.

sections.heading: If you are not approved
paragraphs: If the ADM is minded not to approve you after panel, or to approve you on different terms, you receive a written notice called a qualifying determination, with reasons and the panel's recommendation. In England you then have 28 days either to send written representations to the service, in which case your case returns to the panel, or to apply to the Independent Review Mechanism (IRM), not both.

The IRM is commissioned by the Department for Education and run independently of fostering services by Coram. An IRM panel looks at your case afresh and sends a recommendation to the ADM, who still makes the final decision; the IRM cannot overturn it. It is not open where refusal rests on a specified offence, and it does not handle complaints about a service's conduct.
Wales has its own IRM Cymru, run by Children in Wales. Scotland and Northern Ireland have no IRM; see the nation notes.

sections.heading: After approval: the annual review
paragraphs: Approval is not the end of being assessed. In England, regulation 28 requires a review of your approval within a year and then at least yearly. It gathers the views of you, any child placed with you (according to age and understanding) and any authority that placed a child with you in the past year, and ends with a written report on whether you and your household remain suitable and whether your terms still fit. Council handbooks say it also covers training, any complaints or allegations, health and safety and your safer caring plan.

Your first review must go to panel; later ones go only if the service chooses, often after a significant change or concern. If the service proposes to end or change your approval, the qualifying determination process applies again, with 28 days to respond. You can resign at any time in writing; approval ends 28 days after the service receives your notice.

nations.England: The two-stage assessment, the 10-working-day Stage 1 deadline, the eight-month expectation, the panel, the ADM, the annual review and the 28-day IRM route come from the Fostering Services (England) Regulations 2011 as amended in 2013, the DfE statutory guidance and gov.uk. Gov.uk signposts Fosterline, a free advice line on 0800 040 7675, Monday to Friday 9am to 5pm.
nations.Scotland: The Looked After Children (Scotland) Regulations 2009 apply. Scottish Government guidance says authorities should normally aim to complete an assessment within six months, with enhanced disclosure checks for applicants and household members aged 16 or over, a full medical and at least two references from non-relatives. The decision maker must decide within 14 days of the panel and notify you within seven. There is no IRM: if refused, you can ask within 28 days for a review by a differently constituted panel, with no further right of review. The first review of approval must happen within 12 months, then within three years of the previous one, or sooner to safeguard a child.
nations.Wales: The Fostering Panels (Establishment and Functions) (Wales) Regulations 2018 require an independent chair, a central list including experienced social workers and former foster carers, and reviews of approval within a year and then at least yearly. Foster Wales says the process usually takes around six months. If you are not approved, the 2018 regulations give 28 days for written representations or an independent review application; IRM Cymru, run by Children in Wales, says applicants have 40 days to apply to it, so check the deadline in your own letter.
nations.Northern Ireland: You apply to your Health and Social Care Trust, through HSC NI Adoption and Foster Care, or to an independent agency. nidirect lists training, an application, a GP medical, an AccessNI check and a social services check, references, a social work assessment and a fostering panel recommendation; you can withdraw at any stage. Panels are usual practice rather than a legal requirement, and there is no independent review mechanism: section 126 of the Adoption and Children Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 would allow one, but at the time of writing legislation.gov.uk showed it as not yet in operation.

faq.question: Do I have to attend the fostering panel?
faq.answer: You will be invited and encouraged to go. The Fostering Network says carers should be able to attend for their initial approval and first review, with notice and support to prepare, and councils say you can ask questions as well as answer them.

faq.question: Will a criminal record stop me fostering?
faq.answer: Not automatically. In England only a caution or conviction for a specified offence, broadly offences against children and certain other serious offences committed as an adult, legally bars you or an adult in your household. Anything else is weighed in the assessment; councils advise raising it with your social worker early.

faq.question: Can I be assessed by two services at the same time?
faq.answer: No. Gov.uk says you can only register with one fostering service. You can withdraw and apply elsewhere, but in England a service must ask any service that approved you in the previous 12 months for a reference and, with your consent, can request your earlier records.

faq.question: Can my approval be changed or taken away later?
faq.answer: Yes, with due process. Each review asks whether you and your household remain suitable and whether your terms still fit. If the service proposes to end or change your approval, in England it must issue a qualifying determination and give you 28 days to make representations or apply to the IRM.

title: Types of fostering explained: which kind of foster carer could you be?
standfirst: From emergency and short-term care to kinship, early permanence and Staying Put: what each type of fostering involves, who it suits, and how it shapes your approval, training and pay.

sections.heading: Why fostering comes in different types
paragraphs: Fostering is not one job. Children come into care for different reasons and with different plans, so services describe placements by type: how long the child is likely to stay, what the plan is and what care they need.

You apply and are assessed in much the same way for any of them. What differs is your terms of approval, the training offered and, for some specialist roles, whether a fee is paid on top of the child's allowance. Not every service recruits for every role.

sections.heading: Short-term fostering
paragraphs: Short-term fostering means caring for a child while decisions are made about their future. How long that takes varies: GOV.UK says up to two years in England, the Scottish Government says usually under 12 months, and Foster Wales describes anything from an hour to a year.

The child often has regular contact with their birth family, and the plan may be to go home, move to relatives, be adopted or join a long-term foster family. Your job is to give stability meanwhile and support whatever comes next. It suits people who can live with uncertainty and say goodbye well.

sections.heading: Long-term fostering
paragraphs: Long-term fostering is for children who cannot return to their birth family and for whom adoption is not the right plan. You usually care for the child until adulthood, often as a family relationship for life. Unlike adoption, legal responsibility stays with the local authority, and the child usually keeps some contact with their birth family.
Matching is careful, and long-term homes are often needed for older children and teenagers. In Scotland a child can also live with you permanently under a court permanence order.

sections.heading: Emergency fostering
paragraphs: Emergency carers take children at very short notice, sometimes with less than 24 hours' warning and often late at night or at weekends. The placement is usually for a few nights while the service learns more and arranges something longer. You need to be reachable, flexible and ready with a spare bed, and calm with a child who may be frightened and arrive with very little.

sections.heading: Respite and short breaks
paragraphs: Respite covers two roles. One is looking after a child who lives with other foster carers while they take a break or go into hospital. The other, usually called short breaks, is regular planned care for disabled children or children with additional needs who mostly live at home; a typical pattern is one weekend a month.

Both are often suggested for people who work full time. Respite carers get the same approval, training and support as full-time carers, and short-break carers are matched for their skills and usually get specific training.

sections.heading: Parent and child fostering
paragraphs: A parent, most often a young mother, lives with you together with their baby or young child; the arrangement can begin during pregnancy. The aim is to help the parent build the skills and confidence to care for their child and, often, to assess how they are managing.

You are not usually the one providing day-to-day care: you support, encourage and observe, and your observations feed into the assessment. Placements are time-limited. It suits non-judgemental carers who are comfortable observing, recording and holding clear boundaries.

sections.heading: Sibling groups
paragraphs: Services try to keep brothers and sisters together wherever it is safe, and carers who can take two or more siblings are in steady demand. The law in England and Wales sets a usual fostering limit of three foster children per household, but it does not apply where all the children are siblings of each other.

Space matters. England's national minimum standards say each foster child aged three or over should have their own bedroom; sharing within a sibling group is agreed only after a risk assessment that records the children's wishes.

sections.heading: Fostering teenagers
paragraphs: Many services say they need more carers for teenagers, and misconceptions about young people in care make them harder to place. Fostering a teenager means encouraging independence while keeping boundaries, expecting some mistakes and supporting them through those, backing education and aspirations, and teaching life skills such as cooking and budgeting.
It suits patient, consistent people who will listen and act as an advocate. Some services train existing carers of younger children to move to teenagers.

sections.heading: Therapeutic, specialist and other skilled roles
paragraphs: Specialist therapeutic fostering is for children with very complex needs or behaviour that challenges, often rooted in trauma, neglect or abuse. Carers get support from a trauma-aware team and therapeutic services, and the role usually goes to experienced carers or people with relevant skills. Many services pay a fee on top of the allowance. Other skilled roles include:
bullets: Remand fostering: a home for young people aged 10 to 17 remanded by a court while awaiting trial or sentencing, with dedicated training and assessment.
Unaccompanied asylum-seeking children and young refugees: separated from their families and often distressed; services match language and culture where possible and provide specific training.
Children with disabilities: offered across short-term, long-term, emergency and short-break care.

sections.heading: Fostering for adoption and early permanence
paragraphs: Early permanence covers two arrangements in which approved prospective adopters foster a baby or young child who may later be adopted by them. In fostering for adoption, adoption is the likely plan but legal authority is not yet in place; in concurrent planning, work to return the child to the birth family is still under way.

Carers must already be approved adopters and get adoption pay and leave from the day the child moves in. The trade-off is uncertainty: the child may go home, move to relatives, or the court may refuse a placement order, and carers take the child to regular supervised family contact meanwhile. Services should prepare carers thoroughly and never rush them.

sections.heading: Kinship and connected persons fostering
paragraphs: Kinship fostering (family and friends or connected persons care in England) means a child in the care of the council or health trust lives with someone they already know, usually a relative or family friend. It differs from informal family arrangements, where the council is not involved, and from private fostering (see the FAQ).

Because the child often needs a home at once, English regulations let a council temporarily approve a connected person for 16 weeks, extendable by a further eight in exceptional circumstances, while the full assessment and panel take place. During that time the carer should receive the same allowance as other foster carers. Other legal routes, such as special guardianship, carry different support.

sections.heading: Staying Put and staying on after 18
paragraphs: A foster placement ends at 18, but each nation has an arrangement that lets a young person stay with their former carer: Staying Put in England, When I Am Ready in Wales, Continuing Care in Scotland and Going the Extra Mile in Northern Ireland. The first three run up to 21; Northern Ireland's covers 18 to 21, extended to 25 for those in education, employment or training, though its statutory basis is not yet in force.

After 18 the arrangement is no longer governed by fostering regulations. The Fostering Network reports that there are no minimum post-18 allowances, that many services reduce payments and stop fees, and that some carers face re-approval when the arrangement ends, so ask for the written policy. Supported lodgings, for 16 to 21 year olds leaving care, is a separate role whose hosts are not approved foster carers.

sections.heading: How the type affects your approval, training and pay
paragraphs: When you are approved, the service sets your terms of approval: how many children, their age range and the categories of placement. It can ask you to consider a child outside those terms if that best meets the child's needs, by varying or reviewing your approval. Specialist roles usually need a specific approval, extra training and sometimes previous fostering experience.

Every approved carer receives an allowance for the child's costs, while fee-paid schemes add a payment that recognises the carer's skills. Rates differ by nation and service. Your terms can change as your experience and circumstances do.

nations.England: GOV.UK lists long-term, short-term, family and friends (kinship), emergency, respite and short breaks, remand, parent and child, fostering for adoption and specialist therapeutic care. The usual fostering limit comes from Schedule 7 of the Children Act 1989, connected persons get temporary approval under regulation 24 of the care planning regulations, and Staying Put has been in law since 2014.
nations.Scotland: The Scottish Government describes short-term (usually under 12 months, including short breaks), emergency, interim (under two years), longer-term (over two years) and permanent fostering under a permanence order. Kinship carers of looked after children, and some carers under a Section 11 order, are eligible for the Scottish Recommended Allowance introduced in August 2023, at least the local foster carer rate. Continuing Care lets a young person leaving care from 16 stay with their former carer.
nations.Wales: Foster Wales describes short-term, long-term, short breaks, parent and child, therapeutic, young refugee and supported lodgings roles, and says specialist types need a specific type of approval. The usual fostering limit applies in Wales too, and When I Am Ready, in law since 2016, lets a young person stay with a foster carer up to 21.
nations.Northern Ireland: Fostering is arranged through Health and Social Care trusts. nidirect lists emergency, short-term, short breaks, long-term, kinship, specialist therapeutic and fee-paid fostering. Kinship carers can later apply through panel to become non-kin carers, Going the Extra Mile supports young people from 18 to 21 with their existing carers, and supported lodgings (STAY) covers 16 to 21 year olds.

faq.question: Can I choose which types of fostering I do?
faq.answer: Yes, within limits. Your assessing social worker discusses what interests you, and your approval sets the number, age range and type of children you can care for. Services match placements to that, though they may ask you to consider a child outside your terms.

faq.question: Is there a limit on how many children I can foster?
faq.answer: In England and Wales the usual fostering limit is three foster children in one household. It does not apply where all the children are siblings of each other, and your council can grant an exemption in other cases after considering the children's welfare.

faq.question: Can I do fostering for adoption if I am not an approved adopter?
faq.answer: No. Fostering for adoption and concurrent planning are for people already approved as prospective adopters by a council or adoption agency, who are then temporarily approved as foster carers for a particular child. Carers get adoption pay and leave from the day the child moves in, and must be told clearly that the placement may not end in adoption.

faq.question: What happens to my approval if a young person stays with me after 18?
faq.answer: A post-18 arrangement is not a foster placement, so it is not governed by fostering regulations and does not count towards the usual fostering limit. The Fostering Network reports that some services are unsure about renewing approval for carers with no room for new placements, and that carers may need re-approval when the arrangement ends.

faq.question: Is private fostering a type of foster care?
faq.answer: Not in the sense used here. It is an arrangement between a parent and someone who is not a close relative to care for a child under 16 (under 18 if disabled) for 28 days or more. The council or trust does not place the child, but it must be told and has a duty to assess and monitor the arrangement.

title: Council or independent fostering agency: how to choose
standfirst: How council fostering services and independent agencies differ in regulation, funding, placements, pay and support across the UK, and the questions to ask any service before you apply.

sections.heading: Two routes to the same children
paragraphs: Every foster carer in the UK is approved by a fostering service. In England, Scotland and Wales that is either your local council or an independent fostering agency (IFA). In Northern Ireland most carers foster through their Health and Social Care (HSC) Trust, though agencies exist too.

A council service recruits, assesses and approves carers for children from its own area; the council is the child's corporate parent and holds the care plan. An IFA does the same but has no children of its own to place: it offers its carers to councils that cannot find a match among their own carers or need a specialist placement. IFAs can be profit-making companies, charities or other not-for-profit bodies; in Scotland they cannot be run for profit.

Both routes lead to the same children, and you can only be registered with one service at a time. The sectors are similar in size in England: Ofsted counted 18,415 mainstream council fostering households and 15,020 agency households at 31 March 2025.

sections.heading: How each route is regulated
paragraphs: Both routes are inspected, but differently. In England anyone running an IFA must be registered with Ofsted under the Care Standards Act 2000. Ofsted inspects each agency against the Fostering Services (England) Regulations 2011 and the national minimum standards, and publishes a graded report. Council fostering services are not registered separately; Ofsted looks at them within its wider inspection of the council's children's services.

In Scotland both council and independent services register with the Care Inspectorate. In Wales they are overseen by Care Inspectorate Wales (CIW), and in Northern Ireland the Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority (RQIA) registers independent agencies and inspects both Trust and agency services.

sections.heading: Where the money comes from
paragraphs: A council funds its own fostering service from its children's services budget. When it places a child with an IFA carer it pays the agency a placement fee instead, which must cover the carer's allowance and fee, the agency's social workers and support, and, where the agency is a company, its running costs and any profit. Council-run recruitment hubs say this is why agency placements cost councils more.
Governments in Wales and Scotland have raised concerns that public money can reach shareholders or parent companies rather than children, which is behind the reforms described below.

sections.heading: How children are placed, and why it matters to you
paragraphs: When a child needs a foster home, the responsible council or Trust looks first at its own approved carers. Only if none has the space, skills or location the child needs does it approach IFAs. This is the biggest practical difference between the two routes.

For council carers it usually means shorter gaps between placements and children from your own area, so school, family time and meetings are closer to home. For agency carers it can mean a longer wait for a first or next placement, and children from another council area, sometimes far away, with extra travel. It can also mean a wider pool of referrals, because an agency hears from several councils, and agency carers tend to look after slightly older children.
Neither pattern is better in itself; it depends on how you want fostering to fit around your life.

sections.heading: Allowances and fees
paragraphs: There are two kinds of payment. The allowance covers the cost of caring for a child: food, clothes, travel and pocket money. A fee is an extra payment recognising the carer's time and skills. Every service pays an allowance; none is required to pay a fee, and fees vary widely.

Each nation sets a floor for the allowance (see the nation notes). In England the government publishes a national minimum allowance each year; for 2026 to 2027 it runs from £176 a week for a child under three outside London and the South East to £309 for a 16 or 17 year old in London. In Scotland the recommended allowance is an agreement between government and councils; independent providers set their own allowances and fees.

The body representing IFAs says agency fees tend to be higher, and councils acknowledge this. Compare the whole package: how much is allowance and how much is fee, whether anything is paid between placements, and what changes when a child moves into a new age band. Foster carers register as self-employed and HMRC's Qualifying Care Relief applies; Fosterline gives free advice on tax and benefits.

sections.heading: Support and training
paragraphs: Whichever route you choose, expect a supervising social worker, preparation training before approval, ongoing training, an annual review and out-of-hours contact.

Council carers are typically supported by a council social worker, local training, a local community of carers and direct links to the council's education, health and wellbeing teams. In Northern Ireland, Trust carers have 24-hour social work support, support groups and short breaks. In Wales, Foster Wales offers council carers a National Commitment to consistent training, support and rewards.

Agency support and training vary, so ask. Many IFAs have invested in therapeutic training and extensive ongoing courses. Because agency children often come from further away, training, meetings and family time may be held nearer the child's home area than yours.

sections.heading: The regional fostering hubs in England
paragraphs: If you enquire about council fostering in England you may be answered by a regional hub rather than a single council. The Department for Education funds these through its Fostering Recruitment and Retention Programme, after the 2022 Independent Review of Children's Social Care called for 9,000 more carers. By July 2024 ten hubs covered about 96 of England's 152 councils, such as Foster with us in the North West and Foster for East Midlands.

A hub is a shared front door for the councils in its region. You enquire once, advisers respond and the hub supports you through information events and the early stages before your preferred council carries out your assessment. Hubs recruit for councils only; to compare an agency, approach it separately.

sections.heading: The not-for-profit direction in Wales and Scotland
paragraphs: Wales has gone furthest. Under the Health and Social Care (Wales) Act 2025, no new for-profit fostering service can register from 1 April 2026. From 1 April 2027 existing for-profit agencies cannot approve new carers, and from 1 April 2030 at the latest councils will generally not place children with for-profit providers. The Welsh Government says council and not-for-profit carers will see no change, a child already placed with a for-profit agency carer can stay where that is in their best interests, and carers whose agency closes will need to transfer to a council or not-for-profit service; a transfer protocol recommends the new service pays at least the current allowances and fees for the rest of the placement.

Scotland already requires independent agencies to be voluntary organisations that do not operate for profit. The Children (Care, Care Experience and Services Planning) (Scotland) Bill, introduced in June 2025 and passed by MSPs in March 2026, would require them to be registered charities after an 18 to 24 month transition; 16 of Scotland's 25 agencies already were. England has no equivalent rule.

sections.heading: Questions to ask any fostering service
paragraphs: Ask the same questions of every service you meet, and notice how quickly and warmly each responds.
bullets: Which children do you need carers for now, and what kind of carers are you recruiting?
How are children referred to you, and how long do new carers usually wait for a first placement? For an agency: which councils do you work with?
Where is my supervising social worker based, how many carers do they support, and how often will they visit?
What training is offered before and after approval, and where?
Where do meetings and family time take place, and how far might I travel?
What support is there out of hours, for my own children, and through support groups or buddy schemes?
How many of your carers currently have no child placed with them?
What is the allowance, is there a fee, is anything paid between placements, and what respite is available?
What did your last inspection report say, and can I speak to some of your carers?

sections.heading: Making your decision
paragraphs: Go to information sessions for at least one council service and one agency, read their latest inspection reports and compare the answers. Choose a service close to home, because you will be attending meetings and taking children to school and family time. Assessment takes months whichever route you take (GOV.UK says up to eight months in England; Citizens Advice Scotland says at least six). You can transfer later, but councils advise against moving while a child is placed with you.

nations.England: Ofsted registers and inspects IFAs and covers council fostering within its inspection of the council's children's services. The 2026 to 2027 national minimum allowance ranges by age from £176 to £267 a week outside London and the South East, £195 to £298 in the South East and £205 to £309 in London. Fosterline: 0800 040 7675.
nations.Scotland: Council and independent services register with the Care Inspectorate. Independent providers must already be not-for-profit, and legislation passed in March 2026 would require them to be registered charities. The Scottish Recommended Allowance for 2026 to 2027 is £177.68 a week for ages 0 to 4, £206.71 for 5 to 15 and £283.35 for 16 and over. Fosterline Scotland: 0141 204 1400.
nations.Wales: Services are overseen by Care Inspectorate Wales. Foster Wales is the national network of 22 council fostering teams. For-profit fostering is being phased out between April 2026 and April 2030. The 2026 to 2027 national minimum allowance is £229 a week for ages 0 to 4, £208 for 5 to 15 and £260 for 16 to 17. Fosterline Wales: 0800 316 7664.
nations.Northern Ireland: Fostering is provided mainly by the HSC Trusts, with some independent agencies; RQIA regulates and inspects both. Of 3,999 looked-after children at 31 March 2024, 84 per cent were in foster care. The Fostering Network lists the 2026 to 2027 allowance as £160 a week for ages 0 to 4, £179 for 5 to 10, £200 for 11 to 15 and £235 for 16 and over.

faq.question: Can I be approved by both my council and an agency?
faq.answer: No. You can apply through your council or an independent agency but can only register with one service. You can move between services later.

faq.question: Will I get a child sooner through a council or an agency?
faq.answer: Usually a council, because councils place with their own carers first and approach agencies only when they cannot find a match. Agency carers may wait longer for a first placement. Ask any service how long its new carers typically wait.

faq.question: Do agency foster carers get paid more?
faq.answer: Often, but not always. Agency fees tend to be higher, while every service must pay at least its nation's allowance floor. Compare the full package, including anything paid between placements.

faq.question: Are the regional hubs in England the same as agencies?
faq.answer: No. They are council partnerships funded by the Department for Education to handle enquiries jointly; if you apply through one, a member council assesses and approves you.

faq.question: I foster for a for-profit agency in Wales. What happens to me?
faq.answer: A child already placed with you can stay where that is in their best interests, but from April 2027 your agency cannot approve new carers and by April 2030 councils will generally not place children with for-profit providers. Your agency may convert, continue under restrictions or close; ask about its plans, and Fosterline Wales can advise.

title: Foster carer pay and allowances in the UK explained
standfirst: How the child's allowance differs from the carer's fee, the 2026-27 minimum rates in each UK nation, what is paid between placements, and how tax, National Insurance and benefits work.

sections.heading: Two different payments: the allowance and the fee
paragraphs: Foster carers are not employees and do not get a salary. Your money comes in two parts. The allowance is for the child: it covers the everyday cost of food, clothes, toiletries, travel and activities, and it rises with the child's age. The fee is for you: it recognises your time, skills and experience, and is sometimes called a skills payment or professional fee.

No service is legally required to pay a fee. The Fostering Network says the two elements should be kept separate and clearly labelled, and warns that some services quote one combined package that hides the split; the Welsh Government instructs every provider to keep them apart. Almost all of it is paid per child, per week, and most of it only arrives while a child is living with you.

sections.heading: What services actually pay: the published totals
paragraphs: The minimum allowances below are the floor for the child's costs, not what you receive. Services publish their own weekly totals for one child, usually combining the allowance and your fee. On 27 October 2026 we checked the rates on the websites of 22 independent agencies and 9 council services. The middle agency figure runs from about £460 a week for a newly approved carer to about £652 with experience or for a child with higher needs, within a published range of £400 to £1,000. Councils publish from about £375 to £697, with a wider spread.

Those figures are per child, per week, and only while a child is living with you. They depend on the child's age and needs, your training level and, for councils, a published fee ladder. Our payments page lists every service we checked with a link to its own page, and the pay calculator turns a published figure into a yearly total and shows how much of it is tax-free.

sections.heading: The national minimum allowances for 2026-27
paragraphs: Each UK government publishes a minimum weekly allowance (in Scotland, a recommended one) by the child's age. The Fostering Network notes that paying it is not a legal duty and is not monitored nationally, so treat it as a benchmark rather than a guarantee. The figures below are from the official pages we checked in October 2026.
The Fostering Network argues that all four minimums fall short of a child's real cost; its recommended 2026-27 rates are £251, £343 and £434 a week for ages 0 to 4, 5 to 10 and 11 and over.
bullets: England, 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027 (GOV.UK): London £205 a week for ages 0 to 2, £208 for 3 to 4, £233 for 5 to 10, £266 for 11 to 15 and £309 for 16 to 17; South East £195, £203, £223, £255 and £298; rest of England £176, £182, £201, £227 and £267.

Scotland, 2026-27 (Scottish Government): the Scottish Recommended Allowance (SRA) is £177.68 a week for ages 0 to 4, £206.71 for 5 to 15 and £283.35 for 16 and over, after a 3.8 per cent inflation rise backdated to 1 April 2026.

Wales, 2026-27 (Foster Wales): £229 a week for ages 0 to 4, £208 for 5 to 15 and £260 for 16 to 17. The Welsh Government sets the rate by annual letter to councils and independent providers as the minimum any Wales-registered service can pay.

Northern Ireland: nidirect (updated March 2026) still shows the scale from 1 April 2024: £149 a week for ages 0 to 4, £166 for 5 to 10, £187 for 11 to 15 and £219 for 16 and over. The Department of Health has since published 2025-26 and 2026-27 rates, and The Fostering Network reports a 3 per cent uplift for 2026-27 backdated to 1 April 2026, so check the Department's current scale.

sections.heading: Council or agency: how the money differs
paragraphs: Every child in care is the responsibility of a council (in Northern Ireland, a health and social care trust), which runs its own fostering service and also buys places from independent agencies. Scottish Government guidance explains how it works: a council's contract pays an agency a weekly rate covering the child's allowance, the carer's fee, management costs and extras; the agency then pays its carers and sets its own allowances and fees.

Council schemes usually publish a fee ladder tied to training and experience. Wigan's scheme from April 2026 pays its entry tier exactly the English minimum, with newly approved carers on roughly £296 to £418 a week per child and more for experienced carers; Surrey pays a skills fee of about £113 or £227 a week on top of the allowance. Foster Wales says council carers there typically receive around £400 a week in total.

No official source shows agencies paying more or less across the board. Foster Wales notes that some agencies encourage carers to give up other work. The real difference is often how often you have a child placed and what you get when you do not.

sections.heading: What is and is not paid between placements
paragraphs: The allowance follows the child. Stirling Council says it moves with the child, including to a short-break carer, and Surrey says the same for respite. When a placement ends, the allowance ends.

Whether any fee continues depends on each service's policy. Edinburgh pays full-time carers a retainer for up to four weeks between placements (twelve for specialist carers). Stirling pays a sliding retainer after a placement ends: one week's fee if you are still without a child at three months, rising to six weeks' fee at twelve months. Wigan pays a £150 weekly retention fee for up to four weeks during step-down introductions and an emergency retainer to carers who keep a bed free. Many services pay nothing.

Policies also cover gaps during a placement: Edinburgh, for example, allows a retainer of up to twelve weeks while a carer is suspended during an investigation. GOV.UK says there is no minimum allowance once a young person is old enough to leave care at 18, even if they stay with you, and Scotland's SRA does not cover continuing care.

sections.heading: Tax: how Qualifying Care Relief works
paragraphs: For tax, foster carers are self-employed. GOV.UK says to register with HMRC when you start fostering and file a Self Assessment return each year; Foster Wales adds that only one person per household needs to register.

Most carers pay no tax on fostering income because of Qualifying Care Relief: a fixed amount per household per tax year plus a weekly amount per child. For 2026-27 the fixed amount is £20,440, with £435 a week for each child under 11 and £515 for each child aged 11 or over. GOV.UK shows these figures and the Low Incomes Tax Reform Group dates them to 2026-27 (2025-26: £19,690, £415 and £495). Under the Finance (No. 2) Act 2023 they rise every April with inflation.

Example: a 14-year-old all year and an 8-year-old for ten weeks gives £20,440 plus £26,780 (52 weeks at £515) plus £4,350 (10 weeks at £435): £51,570 tax-free. Allowances, fees and retainers all count as receipts. At or below your qualifying amount your profit is nil, though you still file a return; above it, you pay tax on the excess or deduct actual expenses instead. Part-weeks count as whole weeks, and the fixed amount is scaled by days if you are a carer for part of the year. HMRC's helpsheet is HS236.

sections.heading: National Insurance and your State Pension
paragraphs: Fostering rarely creates a National Insurance bill, but it can leave a gap in your record. HMRC's manual says that since 6 April 2024 nobody is liable for Class 2 contributions: if your fostering profit after the relief is at or above the small profits threshold you are treated as having paid them, and if it is below you can pay Class 2 voluntarily to protect your State Pension. Alternatively, GOV.UK says foster carers may be entitled to National Insurance credits, which the Low Incomes Tax Reform Group explains are Class 3 credits for carers who neither pay nor are treated as paying Class 2. Decide early; gaps are harder to fix later.

sections.heading: Benefits: the headline rules
paragraphs: GOV.UK says fostering can affect your benefits and you must tell whoever pays them that you get a fostering allowance. Fostering payments are not counted as income for means-tested benefits: Foster Wales lists Universal Credit, Housing Benefit and tax credits among those that disregard them. The charity Kinship adds that you cannot claim the child element of Universal Credit or Pension Credit for a foster child, though your own children are unaffected, and Foster Wales notes that a partner's earnings still count and savings above £16,000 rule out Universal Credit. If your foster child gets Disability Living Allowance or Personal Independence Payment, you may be able to claim Carer's Allowance. GOV.UK's fostering pages do not explain how Universal Credit's work-related requirements apply to carers, so use a benefits calculator or ask Fosterline first.

sections.heading: How to compare what services pay
paragraphs: Allowances, fees and policies vary so much that the only reliable comparison is to ask every service the same questions and get the answers in writing.
bullets: The allowance and the fee separately, per child and age band, checked against your nation's minimum.
What the fee depends on (training, experience, type of fostering) and how you move up a level.
What is paid with no child placed, during respite and holidays, if a child is in hospital or missing, and during an allegation.
Extras: birthdays, religious festivals, holidays, first clothing and mileage. Wigan pays separate allowances for these; GOV.UK says you may be able to apply for them.
How many weeks a year carers like you typically have a child placed.
Tax relief is per child per week, so two packages with the same annual total can leave you in different positions.

nations.England: GOV.UK publishes the minimum by region and age and updates it every April; for 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027 it runs from £176 to £309 a week, and you may get more depending on the child's needs, how many children you foster and your skills. Fosterline gives free advice to carers in England.
nations.Scotland: The SRA, agreed between the Scottish Government and councils, covers the allowance only: fees are set by each service, and independent agencies set their own allowances and fees. It does not cover continuing care. Legislation passed in March 2026 provides for annual uprating and more transparent payments, with detail to follow in regulations.
nations.Wales: The Welsh Government sets the minimum by annual letter and requires allowances to be kept separate from fees, which are set locally. All 22 council services operate together as Foster Wales under a National Commitment on training, support and rewards.
nations.Northern Ireland: Health and social care trusts pay the allowance every four weeks under a Model Scheme benchmarked to England's minimums, and nidirect splits it roughly 40 per cent food, 25 per cent household, 18 per cent clothing, 10 per cent pocket money and 7 per cent travel. Some carers also get a fee for particular knowledge and skills. Tax and National Insurance rules are UK-wide.

faq.question: Is fostering pay a salary?
faq.answer: No. Carers are approved, not employed, and are self-employed for tax. You are paid per child per week: an allowance for the child plus, in most services, a fee for you, which no service is legally required to pay.

faq.question: Will I be paid when I have no child placed?
faq.answer: The allowance stops because it is for the child. Some services pay a retainer or part of the fee for a limited period, such as up to four weeks in Edinburgh; many pay nothing.

faq.question: Will I pay tax on my fostering income?
faq.answer: Most carers do not. For 2026-27 Qualifying Care Relief gives £20,440 per household plus £435 a week per child under 11 and £515 per child aged 11 or over, tax-free. You must still register as self-employed and file a return every year.

faq.question: Will fostering affect my Universal Credit?
faq.answer: Fostering payments are disregarded as income, but you cannot claim the child element for a foster child and you must tell the DWP you receive them. Other income and savings count as usual.

faq.question: Do independent agencies pay more than councils?
faq.answer: There is no official comparison. Agencies build their packages from the weekly rate councils pay them; councils publish fee ladders tied to training. Compare allowance, fee, gaps and extras, not one headline figure.
